content_html:
A traditional IRA is an individual retirement account you open yourself, separate from any plan at work. Contributions may be tax-deductible, the investments grow without yearly tax, and withdrawals in retirement are taxed as ordinary income. This calculator projects how a traditional IRA could grow until you retire, shows what it may be worth after tax, and checks how much of your contribution you can deduct under the 2026 income limits.

How to use this calculator

  1. Current age and retirement age: the account grows for the years in between.
  2. Current IRA balance: what you already hold in traditional IRAs. It is treated as pre-tax money.
  3. Annual contribution: the amount you plan to add each year. Tick "Contribute the maximum" to use the full limit for your age every year.
  4. Expected annual return: an assumed long-run average, not a promise.
  5. Current tax rate and tax rate in retirement: your marginal rate today sets the value of the deduction; the retirement rate sets the tax on withdrawals.
  6. Deduction check: open this section if you or your spouse have a retirement plan at work. Enter your filing status and modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) to see how much of each contribution is deductible.

2026 traditional IRA limits

For 2026 you can contribute up to $7,500 to all your traditional and Roth IRAs combined, or $8,600 if you are 50 or older by the end of the year. You also can't contribute more than your taxable compensation for the year. Anyone with earned income can contribute; whether the contribution is deductible depends on workplace plan coverage and income.

Inside a phase-out range the deductible amount falls in a straight line. The calculator multiplies your limit by the share of the range still left above your MAGI, rounds up to the next $10, and applies the IRS minimum of $200.

How the projection works

Each year's contribution is added at the start of the year, and the whole balance then grows by the expected return. The balance after tax assumes everything you withdraw is taxed at your retirement rate, except non-deductible contributions, which were already taxed once. The limits are held at their 2026 levels for every future year, even though the IRS usually raises them with inflation.

The comparison box looks at new contributions only. It asks what the same pre-tax pay would grow to in an ordinary taxable account, where you would first pay tax on the money you invest and then pay tax on the earnings every year.

Worked example

A 30-year-old with $10,000 in a traditional IRA adds $7,500 a year until 65 and earns 6% a year. Their tax rate is 22% today and 15% in retirement, and nobody in the household has a workplace plan.

  • Balance at 65: $962,767, or about $818,352 after tax on withdrawal.
  • Contributions total $262,500 and investment growth adds $690,267.
  • Deducting the contributions saves about $57,750 in tax along the way.
  • The new contributions are worth $753,021 after tax, compared with $517,790 if the same pay went into a taxable account.

If the same person is covered by a plan at work and files single with a MAGI of $85,000, only $4,500 of each $7,500 contribution is deductible in 2026.

Tips

  • Contributions for a tax year can be made until the tax filing deadline the following April.
  • Non-deductible contributions must be reported on Form 8606 so they aren't taxed twice.
  • Withdrawals before age 59½ usually owe a 10% additional tax on top of income tax, with some exceptions.
  • Required minimum distributions start at age 73 for most people today, which limits how long the money can keep growing.

faq.question: How much can I put in an IRA in 2026?
faq.answer: The 2026 limit is $7,500 across all your traditional and Roth IRAs combined. If you are 50 or older by December 31, you can add a $1,100 catch-up contribution, for a total of $8,600. You can't contribute more than your taxable compensation for the year.

faq.question: Can I have a 401(k) and an IRA at the same time?
faq.answer: Yes. Being covered by a workplace plan doesn't stop you from contributing to an IRA. It only affects whether your traditional IRA contribution is deductible, which depends on your filing status and modified adjusted gross income.

faq.question: What happens if my contribution isn't deductible?
faq.answer: You can still contribute. The non-deductible part becomes your basis in the IRA, so it isn't taxed again when withdrawn, though the earnings on it are. You report it on Form 8606.

faq.question: Can a spouse without earnings have an IRA?
faq.answer: Yes. A married couple filing jointly can use a spousal IRA, which lets the non-working spouse contribute based on the working spouse's compensation, up to the same annual limit.

faq.question: Does this calculator include required minimum distributions?
faq.answer: No. It stops at your retirement age. Traditional IRAs require minimum withdrawals once you reach the required beginning age, currently 73 for most people, which the RMD calculator can estimate.
